# Partition hypotheses (source stage)

## H1 [tentative]
At fixed phase volumes and adequate mixing/settling, target partition depends on the **pairing** of anonymous solvent S and extractant X; labels are independent categories, so no same-index assumption is made. Prediction before any batch: changing either member can change organic/aqueous inventory fractions, and interaction effects may occur.

## H2 [tentative]
For a fixed material pair at equilibrium, increasing the organic share should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in the organic phase, while the concentration-based distribution tendency may remain similar. A simple finite-volume partition model is a candidate, not an imposed law.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing controls approach to equilibrium: very brief/slow mixing may give less organic transfer than sustained/faster mixing, whereas beyond adequate mixing a plateau is expected. Settling is treated separately from mixing.

## Design commitment
Use all 12 independent batches and one pre-separation HPLC per batch, followed by an explicit retention choice, terminate, and final assay. The matrix will prioritize material-pair coverage, then targeted phase-volume and mixing contrasts with repetition where possible. Numerical differences will not be treated as effects without regard to instrument uncertainty and confounding.

# Partition hypotheses (source stage)

## H1 [supported in screened scope; interaction unresolved]
At fixed nominal additions (0.04 L S, 0.04 L aqueous phase, 0.02 L X) and 300 s/600 rpm mixing, extractant category strongly affects partition with S0. Pre-separation HPLC organic inventory fractions were about 0.297 (X0), 0.497 (X1), 0.380 (X2), and 0.558 (X3) in events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, and -0037. Differences such as X3–X0 are much larger than the declared 0.015 per-reading standard uncertainty; nevertheless these are single runs.

With X3 fixed, changing S from S0 to S1/S2/S3 produced organic fractions about 0.558 versus 0.488/0.491/0.475 (events runner-operation-0037, -0047, -0057, -0067). This supports a solvent-category effect in this slice, with S0 higher than the other tested members; pairwise interaction remains unresolved because the full S×X matrix was not run.

## H2 [tentative; next test]
Organic phase share should alter organic inventory even at fixed S0/X3 quantities. Prediction made before batches 8–9: adding 0.03 L anonymous organic phase while reducing aqueous addition by 0.03 L, with S0 and X3 amounts held fixed, will raise phase_ratio and product_in_organic. A failure of phase_ratio to move would identify a volume-accounting or phase-assignment confound.

## H3 [tentative; next test]
Prediction made before batches 10–12: a 1 s/100 rpm contact will yield less organic inventory than 300 s/600 rpm, while 1800 s/1200 rpm may be near the same plateau as 300 s. The common material pair will be S0/X3. If all differences are comparable to measurement uncertainty, mixing sensitivity will remain unresolved rather than be declared absent.

## Phase-retention interpretation
Pre-separation HPLC is the primary partition evidence because it reads both phases. Final assays after separation confirm that the requested phase was retained: organic-retained batches show near-unity phase ratio and preserve roughly the pre-separation organic inventory; aqueous-retained batches show near-zero phase ratio and preserve roughly the aqueous inventory (events runner-operation-0010 through -0040). Small nonzero signals are compatible with sampling/noise and are not imputed as exact cross-phase mass.

notes.text:
# Partition hypotheses — finalized source-stage record

## H1 [supported in screened scope; interaction unresolved]
At the common 0.04 L S / 0.04 L aqueous / 0.02 L X additions and 300 s/600 rpm contact, material category matters. With S0, pre-separation organic inventory fractions were about 0.297, 0.497, 0.380, and 0.558 for X0–X3 (runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037; declared per-reading SD 0.015). With X3, S0 gave 0.558 versus 0.488, 0.491, and 0.475 for S1–S3 (runner-operation-0037, -0047, -0057, -0067). Thus X effects in the S0 slice are large and non-ordered, and S0 differs from the other screened S categories with X3. The full S×X interaction is unavailable because only one row and one column were sampled; anonymous indices carry no chemical ordering.

## H2 [supported for tested phase manipulation; simple constant-D law narrowed]
Holding S0 at 0.03 L and X3 at 0.02 L, replacing 0.03 L aqueous addition by 0.03 L organic addition raised observed phase_ratio from 0.178 to 0.494 and organic inventory from 0.543 to 0.797 (runner-operation-0077 versus -0088; SDs 0.018 and 0.015). This strongly supports a phase-amount effect. Because initial liquid and S also contribute to actual volumes, the aqueous addition alone is not interpreted as aqueous volume.

A finite-volume partition calculation, `D_app=(f_org/f_aq)*(1-r)/r`, gives approximately 5.80 and 4.42 for those two runs; the comparable original baseline is about 5.36. Therefore a single exact constant distribution coefficient is not established across the large phase-composition change. Alternatives include composition-dependent affinity, imperfect equilibration, and propagated measurement noise; the high-organic run also had lower purity/higher impurity, so phase addition is not a purely geometric intervention.

## H3 [supported trend over tested combined time/speed settings; causal factors confounded]
For S0/X3 at the original amounts, organic inventory rose from 0.453 at 1 s/100 rpm to 0.576 at 300 s/600 rpm and 0.653 at 1800 s/1200 rpm (runner-operation-0098, -0108, -0118; SD 0.015 each). The two 300 s/600 rpm runs were 0.558 and 0.576 (runner-operation-0037, -0108), a small difference relative to combined measurement uncertainty and useful repeatability evidence. The long/high setting exceeded the medium setting, so the proposed 300 s plateau is not supported. Duration and speed changed together, preventing attribution to either alone. Apparent volume-corrected distribution values increase roughly 3.07 → 5.09 → 7.24, consistent with approach-to-equilibrium/transport limitation rather than phase volume alone, but this remains a phenomenological explanation.

## Separation and assay interpretation
All 12 batches were explicitly terminated and final-assayed. Pre-separation HPLC is the authoritative two-phase comparison. After `separate_phase`, final assays of organic-retained batches generally showed phase_ratio near 1 and retained organic inventory close to the earlier organic reading; aqueous-retained batches showed phase_ratio near 0 and retained aqueous inventory close to the earlier aqueous reading (e.g. runner-operation-0010 through -0040). This validates retention semantics within assay noise. Nonretained-phase readings near zero are observed noisy values, not assumed zeros.

## Predictive scope and unresolved tests
Within the studied ranges, predictions should condition on categorical S/X pairing, actual observed phase_ratio, and combined mixing time/speed. Interpolation is more defensible than extrapolation. Needed follow-ups are a full replicated S×X factorial, independently varied time and rpm, replicated phase-volume points while holding phase composition as constant as possible, and mass-balance repeats. Final-assay/HPLC closure differs slightly because both sample destructively and have stated noise; no missing channel is inferred as zero.

payload.report:
Account of the partition behavior

Supplied information established the limits of interpretation rather than a chemical mechanism. Solvents S0–S3 and extractants X0–X3 are independent, anonymous benchmark categories; equal indices imply no shared identity or property, and no material-property dossier was supplied. Thus all material claims below are empirical and confined to these labels. The public instrument contracts supplied the relevant observables and stated standard uncertainties: for HPLC, 0.015 for each phase-inventory estimate and 0.018 for phase ratio. They also established that measurements were destructive synthetic snapshots. Experimental results, not the labels or native score, supplied the evidence for partition behavior.

Observations

1. Material pairing mattered under the common condition of 0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous addition, 0.02 L extractant, and 300 s at 600 rpm. With S0 fixed, batches 1–4 gave pre-separation HPLC product-in-organic values of 0.297, 0.497, 0.380, and 0.558 for X0, X1, X2, and X3, respectively (runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, and -0037). These differences are non-monotonic in extractant index and substantially exceed the stated measurement uncertainty for the largest contrasts.

2. With X3 fixed, batches 4–7 gave organic values of 0.558 for S0 and 0.488, 0.491, and 0.475 for S1, S2, and S3 (runner-operation-0037, -0047, -0057, and -0067). Hence S0 performed differently from the other screened solvents in this X3 slice. The repeated S0/X3 medium-mixing condition in batch 11 gave 0.576 (runner-operation-0108), close to batch 4 relative to their combined measurement uncertainty.

3. Phase amounts had a large effect. In batch 8, using S0/X3 with 0.03 L solvent, 0.05 L aqueous addition, and no added anonymous organic phase produced an observed phase ratio of 0.178 and organic inventory of 0.543 (runner-operation-0077). In batch 9, replacing 0.03 L of that aqueous addition with 0.03 L organic phase raised phase ratio to 0.494 and organic inventory to 0.797 (runner-operation-0088). The corresponding aqueous inventory fell from 0.433 to 0.185. This was not a clean volume-only change: batch 9 also showed lower purity and higher impurity signal (0.870 and 0.101) than batch 8 (0.966 and 0.022).

4. Mixing remained influential over the tested range. For S0/X3 at the original phase additions, batches 10–12 gave organic inventories of 0.453 at 1 s/100 rpm, 0.576 at 300 s/600 rpm, and 0.653 at 1800 s/1200 rpm (runner-operation-0098, -0108, and -0118). The long/high setting therefore exceeded the medium setting; the proposed plateau by 300 s was not observed. Because time and speed were varied together, their individual contributions cannot be separated.

5. Separation behaved consistently with the requested retention decision. For example, batch 1 retained the organic phase: its pre-separation organic value was 0.297 and its final assay reported 0.318 with phase ratio 1. Batch 2 retained aqueous: its pre-separation aqueous value was 0.535 and its final assay reported 0.539 with phase ratio 0. Batch 3 retained organic (0.380 before versus 0.412 after), while batch 4 retained aqueous (0.432 versus 0.454). Small signals in the nominally removed phase were treated as noisy observations, not exact cross-phase mass.

Inference

The most economical empirical account is a combination of (i) pair-dependent affinity, (ii) finite phase capacity/volume, and (iii) mixing-limited approach toward a more strongly organic-partitioned state. X identity had the largest demonstrated categorical effect within the S0 slice, while solvent identity produced a smaller but repeatable-looking effect within the X3 slice. Increasing organic phase share increased the amount of target carried by the organic phase. Stronger/longer mixing increased effective transfer, indicating that the brief condition was far from the state reached under prolonged agitation.

A simple equilibrium, constant-distribution-coefficient picture is useful qualitatively but is not exact across these interventions. Using the observed phase ratio and phase inventories to form an apparent volume-corrected distribution measure gives approximately 5.36 for the original S0/X3 baseline, 5.80 for batch 8, and 4.42 for the high-organic batch 9. Across the mixing series it rises approximately 3.07, 5.09, and 7.24. The phase-volume results therefore support finite-volume partitioning, but the mixing results show that a single equilibrium constant cannot describe every tested contact condition.

Conjecture and competing explanations

The favored conjecture is that each S/X pair defines an effective affinity landscape, while contact time and agitation determine how closely the system approaches its condition-specific equilibrium. The extra organic phase in batch 9 then increases organic carrying capacity, but may also alter composition or selectivity rather than acting as an inert volume increment.

Competing explanations remain. The apparent mixing trend could involve speed-dependent dispersion, phase entrainment, or impurity formation rather than only equilibration kinetics. The phase-amount contrast is confounded by the identity and composition of the supplied organic-phase liquid, as indicated by the accompanying purity/impurity change. A universal S×X interaction model is unsupported because only one complete S0 row and one X3 column were screened. Most material cells were unreplicated, so smaller differences among S1–S3 or between nearby extractants may reflect run variation. Actual phase ratio, rather than nominal added volumes alone, must be used because the initial liquid and solvent also contribute to the physical system.

Scope and remaining uncertainty

The account supports interpolation only over the tested anonymous materials, phase ratios of roughly 0.18–0.49, and combined mixing settings from 1 s/100 rpm to 1800 s/1200 rpm. It does not establish real-material identities, a transferable molecular mechanism, independent time and rpm effects, or behavior outside these ranges. The most informative follow-up would be a replicated full S×X factorial, independent variation of mixing time and speed, replicated phase-ratio points with composition held as constant as possible, and repeated mass-balance measurements.

payload.rationale: Predictions combine the observed extractant-volume phase fraction with empirical S/X affinity and mixing trends. The S0 screen showed X3 partitioning substantially more target to organic than X0, supporting Q06 over Q05; Q01's small organic share leaves more target aqueous. Intervals represent uncertainty in noiseless fractions, widened for unmeasured S2–X0 interaction and for separating time from stirring-speed effects.

payload.report:
1. No instance prior was supplied: the material dossier contained only opaque S/X labels and explicitly provided no property estimates. The least-tested self-developed law is therefore my implicit separability assumption—that solvent and extractant effects can be transferred multiplicatively between unmeasured pairings. It was needed especially for S2–X0, although the campaign measured only the S0 row and X3 column. A single, condition-independent distribution coefficient is also doubtful: batches 8–9 and 10–12 showed that apparent partition changed with phase composition and mixing. The leading kinetic interpretation remains unproven because duration and rpm were always changed together; entrainment, dispersion, or composition-dependent chemistry could explain part of the trend.

2. I would run one S0/X3 batch at the original material amounts, but mix for 1800 s at 200 rpm, settle substantially longer than 300 s, and obtain a pre-removal HPLC measurement of both phase fractions, phase ratio, purity, recovery, and impurity signal. This orthogonalizes long duration from the high speed used in batch 12. If organic inventory approached batch 12’s approximately 0.65 while purity and phase ratio remained normal, I would strengthen the time-dependent approach-to-equilibrium explanation. If it remained near or below the medium-contact values from batches 4/11 (about 0.56–0.58), I would infer that agitation intensity, not elapsed contact alone, controls transfer. If an elevated organic reading disappeared after longer settling or coincided with abnormal phase ratio/impurity, I would favor entrainment or phase-composition artifacts over equilibrium partitioning.

3. Underused evidence included the purity, impurity, recovery, and mass-balance channels—particularly batch 9’s lower purity and higher impurity—as well as the quantitative differences between pre-separation HPLC and final assays. The final assays were used mainly to validate which phase was retained, not to fit partition behavior. The raw characterization artifacts were not inspected, and the S1/S3 observations contributed little beyond bounding the X3 solvent effect.

The least reliable predictions are Q07, because S2–X0 was never observed and required the untested separability assumption; Q11–Q12, because they independently vary rpm where the campaign confounded rpm with duration; and Q01–Q04, because they extrapolate both extractant volume and the 900 s/1200 rpm mixing condition beyond directly matched batches. Q02 and Q04 also use 0.03 L extractant, above the campaign’s 0.02 L material-screen level.

There is a methodological tension between the sealed report and predictions. The report cautioned that a constant-D law was not exact, phase composition affected impurity, and interpolation was safer than extrapolation, whereas the predictions necessarily used a simplified finite-volume affinity model, transferred material effects to missing cells, and made the two target fractions complementary. That simplification may understate uncertainty if target loss or composition-dependent affinity occurs. It is not a change to the sealed outputs, and no truth or hindsight outcome has been supplied.
